claims.text: Two-neuron chain: in both divisions, preganglionic neurons in the CNS connect to postganglionic neurons in ganglia outside the CNS, whose fibers run to the effector organs.
claims.quote: The sympathetic and parasympathetic systems each consist of 2 sets of nerve bodies: Preganglionic: This set is located in the CNS, with connections to another set of nerves in ganglia outside the CNS. Postganglionic: This set has efferent fibers that go from the ganglia to effector organs
claims.locator: Anatomy of the Autonomic Nervous System

claims.text: Sympathetic outflow: preganglionic cell bodies in the intermediolateral horn from T1 to L2 or L3; ganglia beside the spine: the sympathetic chain plus prevertebral ganglia (superior cervical, celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric, aorticorenal).
claims.quote: The preganglionic cell bodies of the sympathetic system are located in the intermediolateral horn of the spinal cord between T1 and L2 or L3. The sympathetic ganglia are adjacent to the spine and consist of the vertebral (sympathetic chain) and prevertebral ganglia, including the superior cervical, celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, and aorticorenal ganglia.

claims.text: Sympathetic targets: long fibers to smooth muscle of vessels, viscera, lungs, scalp (piloerectors) and pupils, to the heart, and to sweat, salivary and digestive glands.
claims.quote: Long fibers run from these ganglia to effector organs, including the following: Smooth muscle of blood vessels, viscera, lungs, scalp (piloerector muscles), and pupils Heart Glands (sweat, salivary, and digestive)

claims.text: Parasympathetic outflow: from the brain stem with cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X (vagus), and from the sacral cord at S2 and S3; the vagus carries about 75% of all parasympathetic fibers.
claims.quote: The preganglionic cell bodies of the parasympathetic system are located in the brain stem and sacral portion of the spinal cord. Preganglionic fibers exit the brain stem with the 3rd, 7th, 9th, and 10th (vagus) cranial nerves and exit the spinal cord at S2 and S3; the vagus nerve contains about 75% of all parasympathetic fibers.

claims.text: Parasympathetic ganglia: lie within the effector organs (ciliary, sphenopalatine, otic, pelvic, vagal), with postganglionic fibers only 1 or 2 mm long, so responses are specific and localized.
claims.quote: Parasympathetic ganglia (eg, ciliary, sphenopalatine, otic, pelvic, and vagal ganglia) are located within the effector organs, and postganglionic fibers are only 1 or 2 mm long. Thus, the parasympathetic system can produce specific, localized responses in effector organs

claims.text: Overall roles: sympathetic is catabolic (fight-or-flight); parasympathetic is anabolic (conserves and restores).
claims.quote: The sympathetic nervous system is catabolic; it activates fight-or-flight responses. The parasympathetic nervous system is anabolic; it conserves and restores
claims.locator: Physiology of the Autonomic Nervous System

claims.text: Sympathetic effects: raises heart rate and contractility, bronchodilates, increases hepatic glycogenolysis and glucose release, basal metabolic rate and muscular strength, makes the palms sweat, and turns down functions not needed for immediate survival such as digestion.
claims.quote: Increases the following: Heart rate and contractility Bronchodilation Hepatic glycogenolysis and glucose release Basal metabolic rate (BMR) Muscular strength Causes palms to sweat Decreases functions not necessary for immediate survival (eg, digestion)
claims.locator: Table: Divisions of the Autonomic Nervous System

claims.text: Parasympathetic effects: stimulates gastrointestinal secretions and motility (including bowel evacuation), slows heart rate, reduces blood pressure, controls erection.
claims.quote: Stimulates gastrointestinal secretions and motility (including bowel evacuation) Slows heart rate Reduces blood pressure Controls erection
claims.locator: Table: Divisions of the Autonomic Nervous System

claims.text: Transmitters: acetylcholine from all preganglionic fibers, all parasympathetic postganglionic fibers and the sympathetic postganglionic fibers to piloerectors and sweat glands; norepinephrine from most sympathetic postganglionic fibers.
claims.quote: Acetylcholine: Fibers that secrete acetylcholine (cholinergic fibers) include all preganglionic fibers, all postganglionic parasympathetic fibers, and some postganglionic sympathetic fibers (those that innervate piloerectors and sweat glands). Norepinephrine: Fibers that secrete norepinephrine (adrenergic fibers) include most postganglionic sympathetic fibers.
claims.locator: Physiology of the Autonomic Nervous System

claims.text: Horner syndrome signs: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and hyperemia on the affected side.
claims.quote: Symptoms of Horner syndrome include ptosis (drooping eyelid), miosis (constricted pupil), anhidrosis, and hyperemia of the affected side.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Horner Syndrome

claims.text: Horner syndrome causes: disruption of the cervical sympathetic pathway from the hypothalamus to the eye — central (e.g. brainstem ischemia, syringomyelia, brain or cord tumor) or peripheral (e.g. Pancoast tumor, cervical adenopathy, neck and skull injuries, aortic or carotid dissection, thoracic aortic aneurysm).
claims.quote: Horner syndrome results when the cervical sympathetic pathway running from the hypothalamus to the eye is disrupted. The causative lesion may be primary (including congenital) or secondary to another disorder. Lesions are usually classified as either: Central (eg, brainstem ischemia, syringomyelia, brain tumor, spinal cord tumor) Peripheral (eg, Pancoast tumor, cervical adenopathy, neck and skull injuries, aortic or carotid dissection, thoracic aortic aneurysm)

claims.text: Autonomic dysreflexia: usually after cord injury above T6 (unlikely below T10): a noxious stimulus below the injury, most often bladder distention (often a blocked catheter), provokes life-threatening hypertension.
claims.quote: Cord injury is usually above the T6 level, with dysreflexia unlikely to occur after an injury below the T10 level. Life-threatening hypertension is provoked by a noxious stimulus below the level of spinal cord injury; in about 85% of patients, the stimulus is a urologic disorder, such as bladder distention or urinary tract infection. In up to 85% of cases, the cause is bladder distention, often due to a blocked bladder catheter.

claims.text: Dysreflexia mechanism: stimulation below the injury triggers reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction and a rise in BP; the parasympathetic correction cannot travel below the cord lesion, so the hypertension continues.
claims.quote: Visceral or cutaneous stimulation below the level of spinal cord injury provokes reflex sympathetic activity, resulting in diffuse vasoconstriction and an increase in blood pressure (BP). Normally, the increase in BP would stimulate parasympathetic compensation with vasodilation and correction of BP. However, if the spinal cord is injured, the parasympathetic response cannot travel below the spinal cord lesion, and continued vasoconstriction then leads to continued injurious hypertension.
claims.locator: Pathophysiology of Spinal Cord Autonomic Dysreflexia

claims.text: Dysreflexia signs: sudden headache, nausea and vomiting, visual problems, nasal congestion, anxiety; profuse sweating, flushing and piloerection above the injury, dry pale skin below it.
claims.quote: Symptoms of autonomic dysreflexia are variable, intermittent, and usually sudden in onset. They include headache, nausea and vomiting, problems with vision, nasal congestion, and feelings of anxiety and doom. Profuse sweating, flushing, and piloerection occur above the level of spinal cord injury; vasoconstriction with dry, pale skin occurs below the level of injury.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Spinal Cord Autonomic Dysreflexia
